new_statements.quote: Stress is not marked by either Radcliffe-Brown or Man. In none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family (including PGA) is it phonemically relevant. Non-phonemic stress, in all the languages, falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ), extracted text: PDF p. 35 carries footer "22 A GRAMMAR OF AKAJERU" and section "2.2 Stress" reading exactly "Stress is not marked by either Radcliffe-Brown or Man. In none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family (including PGA) is it phonemi-cally relevant. Non-phonemic stress, in all the languages, falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily." (only a layout hyphenation differs). Preface p. x (PDF p. 11) verified: the book "does not, however, include the more extensively documented Akachari variety of North Andamanese, to which we plan to devote a separate monograph." Sec. 1.3 (printed p. 8) verified: Akachari [aci], Akabo [akm], Akakhora [ack] are "the other…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive in every Great Andamanese language; predictable, non-phonemic prominence falls on the first syllable of the root (not of the prefixed word), with the hedge 'at least ordinarily'. The authors assert this for the whole family, i.e. including Akachari, whose corpus (Portman 1887) is unaccented and which they reserve for a separate monograph.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'at least ordinarily'. (Yadav 1985: 196, for present-day Great Andamanese, adds that vocatives and exclamations take a strong final-syllable accent; Temple 1903: 115 adds stress on every long vowel for 'Andamanese' generally.)
new_statements.domain_note: Root-initial in the phonological word; PGA recording note (ch. 4 endnote 7, p. 50) shows word-level initial stress on a prefixed noun. Statement is family-level; no source gives an Akachari-specific stress rule, and Portman 1887, the only sizeable Akachari record, does not mark stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a family-wide generalization ("in none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family.. in all the languages") from the Akajeru grammar (akaj1239), which explicitly excludes the Akachari corpus and treats Akachari, Akajeru, Akabo and Akakhora as dialects of one North Andamanese language. No Akachari-specific stress description exists: Portman 1887, the only sizeable Akachari record, marks vowel quality but not stress. Present-day Great Andamanese (koine under akaj1239/mixe1288; Sare = Cari is one of its four lexical sources; Licho, of Sare background, d. 2020) has independent statements: Yadav 1985: 196 (weak non-phonemic accent, usually first syllable; final in vocatives/exclamations) and Temple 1903: 115 (long vowel or first syllable of root, for 'Andamanese' generally). Catalog should flag the entry as inherited from a family-level statement.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 'Stress', printed p. 22 (PDF p. 35): stress not marked by Radcliffe-Brown or Man; in none of the Great Andamanese languages (incl. PGA) is it phonemic; non-phonemic stress in all the languages falls on the initial syllable of the root, 'at least ordinarily'. Family-wide claim; the book explicitly excludes the Akachari corpus, to which the authors plan a separate monograph (preface p. x); sec. 1.3.1 (pp. 8-9) treats Akachari as the best-attested North Andamanese dialect, documented in Portman 1887.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 'Accent' p. 196: accent very weak, not phonemic, usually on the first syllable; exception: strong accent on the final syllable of vocatives and exclamations. Describes present-day Great Andamanese (Strait Island koine, Kora-group informant), not Akachari.

sources.note: p. 115 (the scanned text): 'Peculiarities of Speech. -- Stress in Andamanese is placed on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem.' Stated for 'Andamanese' generally on South Andaman (Aka-Bea) data; p. 116 says Portman's Kede and Chariar lists are 'to be treated with much caution' and that Northern word-structure is identical with Southern. Older general statement, not Akachari-specific.

sources.note: 'Introductory Grammar' pp. 1-8 gives only 'Pronunciation of the vowels/consonants' (Hunterian system; acute accents mark vowel quality/length, e.g. a as in father, e as in name). No statement on stress or accent placement anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent|stress|emphas: only the Aka-Chariar verbal prefix ngaram 'to emphasize a word'). This is the main primary corpus of Akachari (1000+ headword vocabulary, 100-page phrase book).
